latin: Heri hebdomadis dierum nomina commemoravimus. Hodie mensium<sup>1</sup> et anni temporum nomina inspiciamus.
Mensium nomina ipsi inveniamus opus erit. — Ipse incipiam:
Primus anni mensis Januarius vocatur. Incipientis enim anni januam aperit.
Non a janua, sed a Jano<sup>2</sup> deo nomen suum ducit.
Sequuntur Februarius, Martius, Aprilis, Majus, Junius, Quintilis, Sextilis...
Antiqua dicis! Ignorasne a principibus<sup>3</sup> nostris Julio Caesare et Augusto ultimos duos menses nomina sua duxisse?
Ideoque nunc dicere oportet Julium pro<sup>4</sup> Quintili et Augustum pro Sextili.
Omnium gentium principes nomina facilius<sup>5</sup> quam mores mutant.
Menses tamen sequentes mutati non sunt: September, October, November, December<sup>6</sup>.
Quando incipit ver<sup>7</sup>?
Cum mensis Martii finis appropinquat et cum arbores gemmas proferunt.
Aestas nomen ducit ab aestu<sup>8</sup>, qui vehementem calorem significat.
Autumno folia cadunt, etiam folia<sup>9</sup> vectigalia<sup>10</sup> (quae vectigal solvendum nuntiant).
Hieme nix montes cooperit; lacus gelu constringuntur; tempus est exercitationum hiemalium.
english: Yesterday we recalled the names of the days of the week. Today let's examine (subj.) the names of the months and of the [seasons] (times of the year).
It will be necessary that we find the names of the months ourselves.— I myself will begin:
The first month of the year is called January. Indeed it opens the door of the [incoming] (beginning) year.
[It's] not from door, but from the god Janus [that] it takes (leads) its name.
There follow February, March, April, May, June, Quintile, Sextile…
You are saying old stuff! Do you ignore [that] the last two months took (to have led) their names from our princes Julius Caesar and Augustus?
And that's why we are now meant to say July for Quintile and Augustus for Sextile.
The premiers of all nations change names more easily than customs.
The following months were not changed however: September, October, Novemeber, December.
When does spring begin?
When the end of the month of March approaches and when the trees bring forth buds.
Summer (aestas) takes (leads) its name from "aestus", which means "severe heat".
In the autumn leaves fall, even tax [bills] (leaves [of paper]) (which announce the tax to be paid).
In winter snow covers the mountains; the lakes are frozen with ice; it is the time of winter sports.

footnotes: Mensis, -is, m., parisyllabic, so the genitive plural is in -ium.

Janus, -i, m., Janus, a very old Roman god, who was represented as having a secound face at the nape of the neck, which must have given him a remarkable field of vision! The words for the months are adjectives. Those which belong to the 3rd declension (Aprilis, October, -bris, etc.) from therefore their ablative in -i (Aprili, Octobri).
Princeps, -ipis, is an adjective used here as a noun: the first (or premier of the State).

Facilius, adv., more easily, comparative of facile, easily (cf. L 12); the corresponding adjective is facilis, n. facile; comparative facilior, -ius, easier; superlative (irregular) facillimus, -a, -um, easiest. You can see that the nominative-accusative neuter of the adjective and comparative can be transformed into an adverb. The superlative of the adverb is obtained by replacing with an e the ending of the superlative of the adjective: facillime, most easily.
September, October, etc., come from septem, octo, etc., because there was a time when the year began on the 1st of March, which similarly explains the old Quintilis and Sextilis (quintus, sextus).

Ver, veris, n., the spring (Sp. la primavera); aestas, -atis, f., the summer (Fr. l'été); autumnus, -i, m., the autumn (Fr. l'automne); hiems, hiemis, f., the winter (Fr. l'hiver). Note that the genders of most of these nouns differ from those of their Romance counterparts.
Aestus, -us, m., sultriness (cf. aestuare, L 32, N 2). Note that calor, -oris, is masculine, as calore is in Italian.
Folium, -ii, n., the leaf, sheet, in every sense of these words.

Vectigal, -alis, n., the tax, is a false imparisyllabic (contraction of vectigale, -is) so the singular ablative is in -i, the nominative-accusative plural in -ia and the genitive plural in -ium, like the parisyllabics. However, in phrase 13, vectigalia does not come from the noun, but from the corresponding adjective: vectigalis (n. vectigale), relating to tax, which has otherwise many forms in common with the noun.
comments: And to finish, let's see more closely the 4th declension, which includes:
1st On the one hand, words in -us, mostly masculines; but manus, the hand, socrus, -us, the mother-in-law, and some names of trees (e.g.: quercus, the oak) are feminine.
nom.	exitus, the exit, the outcome.		exitús
2nd On the other hand, some neuter nouns, whose declension differs from the preceding in the nominative and accusative, which are in the singular in -u and in the plural in -ua.
E.g.: cornu, gen. cornús., the horn (also the musical instrument), acc. sg. cornu, nominative and acc. pl. cornua.
N.B.— Some nouns form their dative and ablative plural in -ubus instead of -ibus. Such is the case with lacus which we will see in all its finery in the exercise.

latin: Quando ferias agitis? — Aestivo tempore.
Nos autumnali tempore eas agere malumus.
Dies quidem breviores fiunt, sed sol etiamtunc saepe splendet.
Hospitium in deversoriis facilius invenitur.
Feriis quietis delectamini.
Nos quoque quietem amamus, sed quod volumus, id efficere non semper possumus.
Mense Augusto ab opere vacare debemus.
Dum fabrica clausa manet, operarii et administri simul omnes in ferias abeunt.
Ruri tamen vitam quietam agere possumus.
In lacubus piscamur.
Regio nostra lacuum referta est.
Lacus hujus regionis piscibus referti sunt.
In lacum urinemur!
In lacus urinemini!
E lacu exeunt.
Lacus aqua dulcis est.
Aquam adducunt lacui.
english: When do you take your holidays? — In the summer time.
*We* prefer to take them in the autumn.
The days surely become shorter, but the sun even then often shines.
Lodging is more easily found in the hotels.
You like (are delighted by) quiet holidays.
We too love the quiet, but we can't always do what we want.
We must [take off] (vacate) from work in the month of August.
While the factory remains closed, all the workers and employees depart on holiday at the same time.
In the country nevertheless we can lead a quiet life.
We fish in the lakes.
The fish [from] (of) these lakes are [tasty] (agreeable) to eat.
The lakes of this region are teaming (full) with fish.
Let's dive in the lake.
Let you dive in the lakes.
They come out of the lake.
The water of the lake is fresh (sweet).
This city is near (neighboring to) the lake.
